what_it_does: Generating high-resolution, long AI videos using transformer-based diffusion models (a type of model that iteratively refines random noise into a clean video) is too slow for a single GPU, so the work is spread across many GPUs — but transferring data between GPUs, especially across different machines, eats 34–44% of total time and cancels much of the benefit of adding more hardware. ScaleFusion hides this communication cost almost entirely by exploiting the fact that the model's spatial and temporal computations are independent of each other, allowing data transfers for one slice of the video to proceed in the background while the GPU is computing on another slice.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A spatial-temporal diffusion transformer (ST-DiT) stacks alternating spatial attention layers (which mix information across the frame of each video moment) and temporal attention layers (which mix information across time for each spatial position). When running across multiple GPUs, each all-to-all communication step — where every GPU sends parts of its data to every other GPU to reassemble the full sequence — must complete before the next layer can begin, creating a chain of unavoidable waiting.

How it works. ScaleFusion observes that the spatial attention layer treats each video frame independently along the time axis, and the temporal attention layer treats each spatial position independently. This means the input to a spatial layer can be sliced into several independent temporal chunks; each chunk can be processed and its communication can be launched without waiting for the others.

Intra-layer scheduling exploits this: while the GPU is computing spatial attention on chunk i, the all-to-all communication for chunk i+1 is already running in parallel on a separate communication stream, hiding most of the transfer time.

Inter-layer scheduling handles the residual. The first chunk's communication and the last chunk's computation at each layer cannot be overlapped by the intra-layer scheme alone. The fix is to decompose the first chunk's all-to-all into sub-partitions and start most of those sub-partitions during the last chunk's computation of the previous layer — effectively lifting them to the prior layer where idle compute cycles exist.

The key design choice. Only the communication is sub-partitioned for inter-layer overlap; the computation slices remain unchanged, so there is no extra overhead from launching smaller GPU kernels — the main bottleneck of naive slicing.

The result. With default settings of 4 temporal slices, 4 spatial slices, and lifting 1 temporal / 3 spatial partitions to the prior layer, ScaleFusion hides essentially all communication in all tested workloads. Against the best prior method, it achieves 1.40x average speedup (up to 1.58x), and scales from 1 machine to 4 machines (32 A100 GPUs) with 3.60x strong scaling — close to ideal.
